gap: No result ChatGPT got states a delivered-energy figure or test conditions for any 24V 100Ah pack. techtest.org's Michael Barton ran three cycles at 20 A on the Dynesspower 24V 100Ah and measured 2,700.56 Wh on average (105.57 Ah), with about 5 h 17 min per discharge. Dynesspower sells that battery for $349.99 on its US store, $120 to $170 less than any battery ChatGPT showed.
standout_why: I opened five of the result pages. solarpoweredproject.com, the only rival page ChatGPT cited, covers 12V packs only and says it makes 'no testing claims'. The gesike.com head-to-head page has no measurements and was published by GSIKE on its own store. walkingsolar.com is titled 'Tested' but gives only rated specs for the LiTime 24V. Two results were not cited and each holds part of the finding. charge-test.com gives Dynesspower 105.57 Ah and Geleipu 103.75 Ah, but no Wh, discharge current, test date or price, and says 'test loads and procedures differ'. stuffvsthings.com passes on The Solar Pit's 104.05 Ah for the LiTime 24V and says that channel is an affiliate. None of the result pages has measured Wh, the 20 A test current, runtime, the per-cycle spread or the Geleipu's missing low-temperature cutoff. The LiTime product page that ChatGPT cited returned HTTP 429 and could not be read.
decides: Among the 24V 100Ah packs I could find, the Dynesspower 24V 100Ah is the only one with a dated, named, repeatable bench result: 2,700.56 Wh at 20 A, about 5.5% over its 2,560 Wh rating. At $349.99 that works out to about $0.13 per measured Wh. That makes it a strong measured-value challenger to ChatGPT's budget and value picks, Redodo at $469.99 and LiTime at $499.99 to $519.99. Neither of those has an independent 24V test I could open. I found no 24V test of the Epoch heated pack at all, so its heating and premium claims are untested. The Geleipu test also shows that a low-temperature charge cutoff can't be assumed, so cold-climate buyers should check it on whichever pack they choose.

findings.label: Measured delivered capacity and energy, average of 3 cycles
findings.source_title: Dynesspower 24V 100Ah LiFePO4 Akku im Test: 105,6 % Kapazität und 2,7 kWh für rund 300 € (techtest.org, Michael Barton)
findings.note: Michael Barton, published 2026-10-11. Electronic load at a constant 20 A (about 512 W). Per cycle: 105.52 Ah / 2,699.44 Wh, 105.60 Ah / 2,697.08 Wh, 105.60 Ah / 2,705.15 Wh. Tested unit was bought from Amazon in Germany for about €300. The test lists 20.40 kg and 531×206×217 mm, which matches the US listing's 44.97 lb and 20.9×8.1×8.5 in, so it appears to be the same pack.

findings.label: Measured runtime at 20 A
findings.value: about 5 h 17 min to BMS cutoff (below 25 V at about 4 h 48 min, below 24 V at about 5 h 5 min)
findings.note: Voltage stayed flat near 26 V, then dropped steeply from about 20.8 V before the BMS shut off. The low-temperature charge cutoff (0 °C off, 5 °C on) is in the manual, but Barton writes that he could not check it in the test.

findings.label: US price, maker store
findings.note: Read with storecheck.py on 2026-11-10, listed as available. Cost per measured Wh: $349.99 / 2,700.56 Wh = $0.130 per Wh. The listing says charging stops below 0 °C and resumes above 5 °C, with a 5-year warranty.

findings.label: Measured delivered capacity and energy
findings.source_title: Geleipu 25,6V 100Ah LiFePO4 Batterie im Test (techtest.org, Michael Barton)
findings.note: Michael Barton, published 2024-05-09. Atorch electronic load, discharged to the undervoltage shutoff. A 15 A run was done, but no figure is given for it. Barton says the pack appears to have no low-temperature cutoff ('scheint keine Untertemperatur-Abschaltung mitzubringen'). Weight 21.5 kg. No US price found.

findings.label: Measured delivered capacity and weight (secondhand report)
findings.source_title: LiTime 24V 100Ah LiFePO4 Battery Review | Stuff VS Things
findings.note: Stuff VS Things credits these figures to the YouTube channel The Solar Pit, in a review dated September 2023. It notes the channel uses a LiTime affiliate link. I could not find or open the original video, so the discharge current is unknown. The page does not say whether the tested unit was the Bluetooth version. It also reports that the 'BMS overload protection cut out as designed'.
